system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel — Seller Update Review & Countermeasures

## Executive Summary

The Seller's package deviates from our playbook across **four distinct strands**, each materially adverse. Three of them fall outside the [STANDARD] category entirely (general cap, thresholds, time limit) — confirming we should treat this as an untrusted draft, not a settled position. Together they reduce our warranty exposure, weaken our rights to know, and carve out core protections. I recommend taking firm but principled pushback; this is recoverable because the positions appear negotiated from the Seller side without our prior principal sign-off, and the commercial stakes are real.

---

## Material Departures and Pushback Recommendations

### I. General Warranty Cap — 20% Without Principal Approval

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Cap % | Starting 25% / AUD 6,000,000 | 20% / AUD 4,800,000 |
| Approval | Requires Amelia Frost's prior written authority identifying the draft | None stated |

**Pushback:** Demand the cap remain at 25% (AUD 6,000,000) unless and until Amelia Frost provides written confirmation specifying the draft reference. A 20% cap with no principal approval is a step backward and creates asymmetry risk if Harbourglass ever insists on the lower number in later rounds.

**Reasoning:** Even accepting the 20% figure outright is premature. Our lead counsel (Daniil) has told us repeatedly that the 20% is *conditional* on prior written authority from Amelia Frost. That condition has not been satisfied. Leaving it unconditional shifts burden onto us without commensurate seller gain. We lose AUD 1,200,000 of warranty cap if something goes wrong post-close.

---

### II. Thresholds — de minimis AUD 25,000; Basket AUD 250,000

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| De minimis | AUD 5,000 | AUD 25,000 |
| Basket | AUD 50,000 — seller liable from first dollar once exceeded | AUD 250,000 — liability only triggers at 250,001 |

**Pushback:** Restore de minimis to AUD 5,000 and basket to AUD 50,000 (seller liable from first dollar above the basket). The threshold gap is exactly 5× for both figures — the kind of gap that opens up liability precisely when it should not flow through.

**Reasoning:** Under the seller's terms, a small claim that is less than AUD 25,000 is simply non-actionable, no matter how significant. But the buyout price is AUD 24,000,000 — a claim worth AUD 25,000 is one of the largest possible deals. Re-leveling the de minimis and basket gives us real protection for the most impactful claims. On the basket alone, seller liability under AUD 50,000 thresholds starts *immediately* above AUD 50,000 — meaning a claim just barely over that amount costs the seller nothing if it remains under AUD 250,000. The seller's AUD 250,000 basket means half that or more can sit untouched.

---

### III. Time Limit — 18 Months Without Principal Approval

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| General claims period | 24 months standard; 18 months fallback requiring Amelia Frost written approval | 18 months, unconditional |

**Pushback:** Preserve the 24-month general claims period. The 18-month figure requires prior written approval from Amelia Frost identifying the draft, which has not been provided. We should resist adopting the shorter period unilaterally.

**Reasoning:** A standard SaaS tail of 24 months protects us for materially longer than 18 months. If Harbourglass offers 18 months purely to compress exposure, that's a tactic to reduce their tail risk at our expense without our permission. Treat it the same as the cap situation — there is a going-in right to this provision and we cannot waive it without our principal's hand.

---

### IV. Fundamental / Title Claims Subject to General Caps and Limits

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Regime | Separate — 100% cap, at least six years, outside basket/de minimis/knowledge bar | Same caps and time limits as general warranties |

**Pushback:** Fundamental and title claims must remain in a separate regime with a 100% cap, a minimum six-year window, and operation outside the de minimis, basket and knowledge provisions. Administrative simplicity for the seller is not a reason to sacrifice fundamental rights.

**Reasoning:** A breach of title, capacity, or regulatory licence is categorically different from a general operational defect. Treating it identically to a routine warranty erodes the full protection we need. The six-year minimum also aligns with the age of the assets and the typical accrual pattern of latent title defects in data-centre and telecom infrastructure.

---

### V. No Fraud / Wilful Concealment Carve-Out

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Fraud, wilful concealment, deliberate misconduct | Carved out of *all* caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies, and non-reliance — maximum enforceable | Not carved out |

**Pushback:** Insert explicit exceptions for fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct *before* the limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance clauses, giving them the same force as the general limitation provisions. These carve-outs shall survive any general waiver.

**Reasoning:** This is foundational to our position and we will not waive it. Without it, Harbourglass could suppress critical facts during due diligence, rely on the resulting exclusion to shield themselves, and then fund any claim against us through a cap that excludes what they cannot define as concealment. The carve-out must be explicit and survive modifications. No waiver, full stop.

---

### VI. Blanket Buyer-Knowledge Exclusion

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Clause 8.3 | Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity | "No claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records." |

**Pushback:** Delete the blanket exclusion. Replace with: *"No Seller has knowledge of anything that would ordinarily come to the attention of a reasonable enquiry agent reasonably engaged to conduct enquiries into matters of concern to the Buyer. To the extent any Seller possesses such knowledge, the Buyer may require the seller concerned to make a specific disclosure to its named knowledge person(s), together with supporting documentation, as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the matter."*

**Reasoning:** The seller's version reads like a complete release of the buyer's information rights — specifically the discovery of data-room contents and public registers. This is the opposite of what our playbook demands. Any exception buried inside it still suppresses disclosure, and we do not accept that tradeoff. Named seller knowledge persons plus reasonable-enquiry obligations are the minimally viable framework.

---

### VII. Whole-Data-Room and Public-Register "Deemed Disclosure"

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Schedule 7 / Disclosure Letter | Require *specific* fair disclosure; reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure | Relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers |

**Pushback:** Amend Schedule 7 so disclosure is limited to facts *specifically* identified in the Disclosure Letter, with each item supported by the indexed data room records cited (DD-002 through DD-012). Do not capture the entire data room or every publicly searchable record as "disclosed." Add a specific fair-disclosure obligation requiring support and documentation.

**Reasoning:** "General disclosure of the data room" is an open-ended statement that potentially covers everything in 14 documents. Our playbook requires *specific* disclosure tied to facts, dates and events — otherwise disclosure becomes noise and silences legitimate findings. Restricting the scope to items we have already been asked to evaluate gives us fairness and control.

---

### VIII. Bluefen Change-Control Consent — Satisfied on Delivery

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Conditions | Effective consent AND evidence that conditions are satisfied *before* Completion | Consent satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent"; uses reasonable endeavours |

**Pushback:** Write *"Effective Bluefen change-control consent, together with evidence that all conditions attaching to the consent (including compliance with any change-control conditions in DD-002 and DD-007) have been fully satisfied by the Seller prior to Completion, is a condition precedent to Completion."*

**Reasoning:** A customer consent obtained during closing but already satisfied before signature does not satisfy a "condition precedent" requirement for a material customer — especially for a customer whose services are central to our acquired systems (FY26 revenue ~30%). The Consent Letter confirms the Seller has neither a final written consent nor evidence of satisfied conditions as of the letter date. We cannot allow Condition Precedent to default to "on delivery."

---

### IX. Riverlark Facility — Post-Completion Release

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Status | Current payout from Completion funds; direct repayment; effective security releases; post-completion release requires irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval | Release "to be provided following Completion" |

**Pushback:** Ensure the facility is repaid from Completion funds (or meets the buyer's equivalent payout requirement), with an immediate effective discharge of security releases attached to the Completion deed. If discharge cannot be secured before signature, insert the irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval mechanism as a backstop, per our playbook.

**Reasoning:** The deferred release converts a pre-completion condition into a post-completion obligation. It gives Harbourglass plausible deniability if payments stall. We want certainty on Day One of operations.

---

### X. DD-005 Employee Bonuses Excluded from Funds Flow

| | Our Position | Seller |
|---|---|---|
| Funds flow | A
=== END ADVICE ===
